documents.unit: AI Resource Hub / AI Working Group
documents.title: Santa Clara University AI Guidelines
documents.summary: Santa Clara's university-wide guidelines cover data confidentiality, accuracy checking, bias, IP, procurement through the TAR process and AI in research for all staff, students and faculty. They quote the Provost that there is no university-wide AI policy for courses: faculty decide and must communicate their rules, and AI detectors are to be used with care.
documents.stance_why: For coursework the page quotes 'the University does not have a university-wide policy for AI use across courses and curricula' and says 'Faculty are expected to clearly communicate their policies', so the decision goes to instructors, which is delegates; the rest of the document sets general duties (data, accuracy, citation) that do not choose a stance on student AI use.

units.why: The page calls itself a 'work in progress' that changes 'as the technology, the law and the University community usage evolves', so the rules are provisional; this is P54 and the speaker is the institution (all).
units.anchor: as the technology, the law and the University community usage evolves

units.why: The Purpose section says SCU 'is committed to actively and ethically engaging' with AI in line with its mission; this is an institution-level statement of purpose, so P56 and informs.
units.anchor: is dedicated to advancing knowledge and learning, and is committed to actively and ethically engaging

units.why: A working group 'convened to specifically address AI in administrative areas' and another to 'develop resources and guidelines around the use of AI in teaching' describe institutional set-up, so before-course governance; P56 is the nearest type (no type for working groups).
units.anchor: will work in parallel with a working group of faculty and staff that will develop
units.fit_note: Describes the two working groups (administrative and teaching) rather than a framework of principles.

units.why: 'we must also use AI in a manner that is consistent with University policies and applicable laws' is a binding duty to follow existing law and policy, so P77 with must.
units.anchor: use AI in a manner that is consistent with University policies and applicable laws

units.why: The risk list says if AI 'is given access to personal information, the technology may not respect the privacy rights of individuals'; a fact about privacy risk, so P50 and informs.
units.anchor: if an AI tool is given access to personal information, the technology may not respect

units.why: The risk bullet says confidential information given to AI means 'the University may lose its intellectual property (“IP”) rights'; it concerns IP and confidentiality loss, so P52 (copyright and ownership) fits best, and P50 (data protection) is the second option but the stated harm is loss of IP.
units.anchor: the University may lose its intellectual property (“IP”) rights to that information

units.why: 'AI outputs may violate the IP rights of others, and might not themselves be protected by IP laws' is a fact about ownership and copyright of AI output, so P52 informs.
units.anchor: AI outputs may violate the IP rights of others, and might not themselves be protected

units.why: 'AI outputs might be factually inaccurate, and we might be exposed to liability if we rely on those outputs' warns that output can be wrong, so P31 informs.
units.anchor: AI outputs might be factually inaccurate, and we might be exposed to liability if we

units.why: 'AI may produce decisions that are biased, discriminatory' names bias as a harm, so P53 informs.
units.anchor: AI may produce decisions that are biased, discriminatory, or otherwise inconsistent with our policies

units.why: The Scope section says the guidelines cover use 'by faculty, researchers, postdoctoral scholars, staff, students, volunteers, and trainees'; a definition of who and what is covered, so P61 with informs.
units.anchor: provide guidance on the use of AI tools by faculty, researchers, postdoctoral scholars, staff, students,

units.why: 'community members are encouraged to regularly review the most recent version' because guidelines 'may be updated from time to time'; a statement that the policy changes, so P54 with should.
units.anchor: SCU community members are encouraged to regularly review the most recent version of these Guidelines

units.why: 'SCU expects all SCU community members to follow these guidelines when using AI tools for teaching and learning, research, and work-related functions' sets the binding framework and its principles for the whole institution, so P56.
units.anchor: SCU expects all SCU community members to follow these guidelines when using AI tools for

units.why: Community members must 'Complete the Technology Acquisition Request (“TAR”) process and obtain TAR approval before purchasing' AI products; this is an institutional review of vendors, so P65, although it is a duty on the purchaser rather than a review policy.
units.anchor: obtain TAR approval before purchasing (or acquiring for free) AI products
units.fit_note: Binds the person acquiring the tool to a TAR review (cybersecurity, vendor risk, legal, accessibility); P65 describes institutional review of contracts.

units.why: 'must not enter Level One Data or Level Two Data ... into any public or unapproved AI tool' is a ban on putting protected data into AI, so P50 with must-not and restrict (allowed only for approved tools).
units.anchor: must not enter Level One Data or Level Two Data

units.why: 'may enter Level Three Data into public AI tools' is an explicit permission tied to a data classification, so P50 with may.
units.anchor: SCU community members may enter Level Three Data into public AI tools

units.why: 'Any information provided to public AI tools may be stored, reused, or disclosed by the provider and should be treated as public' explains why privacy matters (AI tools store prompts), so P50 informs.
units.anchor: may be stored, reused, or disclosed by the provider and should be treated as public

units.why: Members 'must verify and validate each element of output from AI tools to ensure there is a human audit'; users must check AI output, so P31 with must.
units.anchor: must verify and validate each element of output from AI tools

units.why: 'AI generated content may be inaccurate, incomplete, or fabricated (sometimes called “hallucinations”), including citations that do not exist' states that output is often wrong, so P31 informs.
units.anchor: AI generated content may be inaccurate, incomplete, or fabricated

units.why: Users 'are responsible for any content published that includes AI-generated material': ownership of what is released, so P29 with must.
units.anchor: are responsible for any content published that includes AI-generated material

units.why: Users 'should regularly stress test their AI tools' to learn the limits of the tool; closest is P31 (understanding that AI errs) but it is about testing the tool, not checking one output.
units.anchor: users should regularly stress test their AI tools
units.fit_note: Advises probing the tool with simple and expert-level queries to learn its limits, which P31 does not mention.

units.why: Members 'must consider whether the data input into, and the output of, AI tools produces decisions that may result in a disparate impact'; a duty to check output for bias, so P53, which names bias as a concern.
units.anchor: Do not rely on any output that is indicative of a potential bias
units.fit_note: Imposes a duty to check output for disparate impact on protected classes and not rely on biased output; P53 only names bias as a concern.

units.why: 'Do not represent AI-generated content as solely your own work where credit or sourcing is required (e.g., academic submissions ... source coding)' limits claiming AI output as one's own; nearest is P24 (credit AI use) since it is conditioned on credit being required.
units.anchor: Do not represent AI-generated content as solely your own work where credit or sourcing is
units.fit_note: Phrased as a ban on passing off AI content as solely one's own where credit is required, naming academic submissions and source code, rather than as a disclosure statement.

units.why: Where an option exists 'SCU community members are expected to exercise it and opt out of training'; a data-protection step, so P50 with should.
units.anchor: SCU community members are expected to exercise it and opt out of training

units.why: Members 'are encouraged to use structured prompting frameworks with more tailored prompting'; advice on using AI effectively, so P44 with encourage, although it is not framed as a professional skill.
units.anchor: encouraged to use structured prompting frameworks with more tailored prompting
units.fit_note: Recommends structured prompting for better output quality; P44 is about effective AI use as a professional skill.

units.why: 'The Information Services team intends to publish a list of specific applications that have been vetted' signals university-vetted tools, so P50 (prefer vetted tools) informs.
units.anchor: intends to publish a list of specific applications that have been vetted by the University

units.why: Members 'should only enable Zoom AI Companion and other TAR approved tools with contractual protections' limits AI meeting assistants to approved tools; this is an operational (non-teaching) use, so P76 with should.
units.anchor: should only enable Zoom AI Companion and other TAR approved tools with contractual protections

units.why: 'Only begin recording once all participants have consented' is a consent rule for AI meeting assistants in operations, so P76 with must.
units.anchor: Only begin recording once all participants have consented

units.why: 'If confidential data will be discussed, AI meeting assistants must not be used' bans a tool where confidential data is present; a data-protection rule so P50, although the setting is meetings (P76 was the other candidate, but the harm named is confidentiality).
units.anchor: If confidential data will be discussed, AI meeting assistants must not be used

units.why: The coursework section says deep learning 'could be undermined with the utilization of AI-generated content being passed off as one's own work'; a reason, so P41 (AI shortcuts learning) informs.
units.anchor: intellectual honesty and scholarly integrity, and deep, critical learning which could be undermined
units.fit_note: Frames the concern as integrity and deep critical learning being undermined by passing off AI content as one's own.

units.why: Quoting the Provost, 'the University does not have a university-wide policy for AI use across courses and curricula'; the decision rests with faculty, so P04 with informs.
units.anchor: the University does not have a university-wide policy for AI use across courses and curricula

units.why: 'The faculty have a responsibility to weigh the humanistic, ethical, and pedagogical considerations when determining how and whether to integrate AI' places the choice with instructors, so P04 with should.
units.anchor: The faculty have a responsibility to weigh the humanistic, ethical, and pedagogical considerations

units.why: The goal 'to ensure that AI is facilitating and not replacing learning' states that AI must not replace the student's learning; nearest is P32 (AI must not replace thinking) though the duty is placed on faculty.
units.anchor: to ensure that AI is facilitating and not replacing learning, is accessible to students
units.fit_note: The duty is on faculty to ensure AI facilitates rather than replaces learning and is accessible to students (equity), not on students.

units.why: 'Faculty are expected to clearly communicate their policies and rationales for AI use in their courses and assignments' requires instructors to state their rules and reasons, so P09 with should; the rationale element goes beyond P09.
units.anchor: Faculty are expected to clearly communicate their policies and rationales for AI use
units.fit_note: Requires communicating both the policy and its rationale in courses and assignments, not only a syllabus statement.

units.why: Faculty 'expect students to maintain academic integrity and live up to student codes of conduct' ties AI use to existing student rules, so P77 with must for students.
units.anchor: expect students to maintain academic integrity and live up to student codes of conduct

units.why: 'there are risks of misidentification, which can have consequences in the classroom' about detection software says detectors can be wrong, so P39 (do not rely on detectors) informs.
units.anchor: there are risks of misidentification, which can have consequences in the classroom

units.why: Detection tools 'are best used with careful consideration and as one of many ways to work with students': a limit on their use, so P39 with should (they are not banned).
units.anchor: best used with careful consideration and as one of many ways to work with students
units.fit_note: Does not say detectors are unreliable or banned; says use them with care and as one source among many.

units.why: 'include the use of these tools in any discussion with students around course policies, making clear why and how such services may be used' asks instructors to tell students about detector use, so P66 (explain and discuss rules) with should.
units.anchor: include the use of these tools in any discussion with students around course policies
units.fit_note: Specifically about being transparent with students about why and how detection tools are used.

units.why: 'Establishing clear escalation language, processes, and guidelines in the event of detected plagiarism, at the department level is important' asks departments to set escalation procedures; no type covers department-level escalation procedures, so UNCOVERED rather than P36 (which classifies misuse as misconduct).
units.anchor: Establishing clear escalation language, processes, and guidelines in the event of detected plagiarism, at the
units.uncovered_note: Departments should set clear escalation language and processes for suspected or detected plagiarism.

units.why: Conversations 'in an open and educational manner (especially given the number of false positives)' mean talking with students before treating a case as misconduct, so P57 (talk before escalating); P68 (educative response) is related but the stress is on the conversation.
units.anchor: initiate and engage in such conversations with students in an open and educational manner

units.why: 'AI detection should be treated as a guideline and not a grading metric' sets how a detector result may be used as evidence, so P69 (evidence standard) with should; P39 was used for reliability, this one is about the standing of the result.
units.anchor: AI detection should be treated as a guideline and not a grading metric
units.fit_note: Says detection output is a guideline and not a grading metric; it does not set a proof standard.

units.why: In research, 'individuals who use AI in research should be transparent regarding its use'; a disclosure rule for research, so P62 with should.
units.anchor: individuals who use AI in research should be transparent regarding its use

units.why: 'Researchers are responsible for the accuracy of any content created by AI that is included in any research output' makes researchers answerable for AI content in research outputs, so P62.
units.anchor: Researchers are responsible for the accuracy of any content created by AI

units.why: 'Researchers are expected to follow the policies of journals, funding agencies and professional societies' defers to venue and funder rules, exactly P62.
units.anchor: Researchers are expected to follow the policies of journals, funding agencies and professional societies

units.why: 'Researchers must avoid uploading ... any unpublished research data or other confidential information into an unauthorized AI tool'; a confidentiality ban, so P50 (P62 is the other candidate, but the rule is data protection).
units.anchor: Researchers must avoid uploading, or using as input, any unpublished research data or other confidential

units.why: 'The National Institutes of Health (NIH) and U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), among others, prohibit using AI tools for peer review' reports funder rules on peer review, so P62 informs.
units.anchor: NIH) and U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), among others, prohibit using AI tools for peer

units.why: 'inputting interview data into an unauthorized AI tool ... creates the possibility that quotations or other information from research subjects could become public' protects research subjects' personal data, so P50 informs.
units.anchor: inputting interview data into an unauthorized AI tool to perform preliminary analysis creates the possibility

units.why: 'Researchers should be mindful that the output of AI tools may infringe the rights of third parties' flags copyright risk of AI output, so P52 with should.
units.anchor: the output of AI tools may infringe the rights of third parties

units.why: 'Researchers should comply with the expectations of their respective school, department and sub-discipline, as well as journal and/or publisher requirements' defers to unit and venue rules for research, so P62 with should.
units.anchor: Researchers should comply with the expectations of their respective school, department and sub-discipline

units.why: 'Citing AI tools used and clearly explaining their specific contributions rather than presenting AI-generated content as your own work' is a citation duty for research, so P24 with should.
units.anchor: Citing AI tools used and clearly explaining their specific contributions

units.why: 'creating an audit trail by tracking the AI tools used, prompts, exact steps taken to independently verify' asks researchers to keep a record of tools, prompts and verification, so P26 (keep logs), though it is not submitted to anyone.
units.anchor: creating an audit trail by tracking the AI tools used, prompts, exact steps taken
units.fit_note: Records are for verifying AI-generated citations in research; the page does not say they are submitted.

units.why: 'All University research is subject to the University’s research integrity policies, such as the Policy on Research Misconduct' puts AI-related research under existing policy, so P77.
units.anchor: All University research is subject to the University’s research integrity policies

units.why: Members 'should always keep in mind the usual rules and policies concerning privacy, honor code, academic integrity, research conduct, information security' ties AI use to existing rules, so P77 with should.
units.anchor: should always keep in mind the usual rules and policies concerning privacy, honor code, academic

units.why: 'Students should review the policies relating to academic integrity in the Student Conduct Code' directs students to the conduct code that governs AI misuse, so P77 for students.
units.anchor: Students should review the policies relating to academic integrity in the Student Conduct Code

units.why: 'the University's specific schools may also have additional rules and policies' says the layers add rules; no type covers layering of school rules on top of university rules, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: the University's specific schools may also have additional rules and policies
units.uncovered_note: Schools may add their own AI or integrity rules on top of the university guidelines.

documents.title: AI Syllabus Policy
tiers: Generative AI permitted (examples: specified graded assignments, ungraded work, self-study, case-by-case permission, not on tests)
documents.summary: A library guide for faculty stating that SCU has no campus-wide AI policy and giving sample syllabus language for courses that permit AI and courses that do not. It also lists parameters such as attribution, responsibility for output and not entering others' private data.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'Santa Clara University currently does not have a campus wide AI policy' and 'Faculty are encouraged to determine how AI tools and systems are utilized in their classrooms', and offers permitted and not-permitted sample statements, so it hands the choice to instructors: delegates.

units.why: 'This page provides suggestions on how you could possibly format your AI policy statement ... to help you determine the best fit for your classroom' shows that the page leaves the choice to each instructor, so P04 informs.
units.anchor: provides suggestions on how you could possibly format your AI policy statement

units.why: The page created by the 'Faculty Collaborative for Teaching Innovation' 'aims to assist faculty with navigating AI'; a support resource for faculty, so P63 informs.
units.anchor: Created by the Faculty Collaborative for Teaching Innovation at SCU, this page aims to assist

units.why: 'Santa Clara University currently does not have a campus wide AI policy' states the institutional position that no single rule exists, so P04 informs.
units.anchor: Santa Clara University currently does not have a campus wide AI policy

units.why: 'Faculty are encouraged to determine how AI tools and systems are utilized in their classrooms and communicate this to their students' leaves the decision to each instructor, so P04 with should.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to determine how AI tools and systems are utilized in their classrooms

units.why: 'by not having an AI statement in your syllabus you create ambiguous expectations for students which can lead to misunderstandings and stress' urges every syllabus to include an AI statement, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: by not having an AI statement in your syllabus you create ambiguous expectations for students

units.why: 'your goal is to be as clear and direct as possible to avoid ambiguity' sets a standard for how the statement is written, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: your goal is to be as clear and direct as possible to avoid ambiguity
units.fit_note: About the clarity of the statement rather than whether one must exist.

units.why: Sample text 'Graded assignments with specified Generative AI tools are allowed, as described in the syllabus' allows AI assignment by assignment, so P04 (per-assignment rule) with may.
units.anchor: Graded assignments with specified Generative AI tools are allowed, as described in the syllabus

units.why: 'we will go over in class how to access and use them' has the instructor teach the allowed tools in class, so P66 (discuss AI with students); P44 is also possible but the stress is explaining the tools and their privacy issues.
units.anchor: we will go over in class how to access and use them
units.fit_note: Sample promise to teach access and use of the permitted tools in class.

units.why: 'Ungraded assignments are allowed because students can augment their learning outside of class' permits AI on ungraded practice work, so P14 (practice and study aids); the sample does not name study aids specifically.
units.anchor: Ungraded assignments are allowed because students can augment their learning outside of class
units.fit_note: Permits AI on ungraded assignments generally, without listing practice problems or study guides.

units.why: 'still need to demonstrate mastery of skills without the support of Generative AI on graded assignments' bans AI on graded work in this sample, so P01 with must-not.
units.anchor: still need to demonstrate mastery of skills without the support of Generative AI on graded

units.why: 'Self-study outside of the classroom is allowed because Generative AI can enhance learning' permits AI for self-study, so P12 (AI as a tutor for understanding).
units.anchor: Self-study outside of the classroom is allowed because Generative AI can enhance learning

units.why: 'Use of AI is only allowed under special circumstances in which individual students approach the instructor on a case-by-case basis' sets permission case by case, so P04, with a restrictive default.
units.anchor: individual students approach the instructor on a case-by-case basis to develop a learning approach
units.fit_note: Sample is a restrictive default with individual exceptions negotiated with the instructor.

units.why: 'it is not allowed to be used during open book/note tests or quizzes' bans AI during tests even when it is allowed elsewhere, so P22 with must-not.
units.anchor: it is not allowed to be used during open book/note tests or quizzes

units.why: 'if you are found to be using unpermitted resources during these exercises you will be violating the university's Student Code of Conduct' classifies test-time AI use as a code violation, so P36.
units.anchor: you will be violating the university's Student Code of Conduct

units.why: 'It is never acceptable to completely copy the work of generative AI' bans submitting AI output as is, so P19 with must-not.
units.anchor: It is never acceptable to completely copy the work of generative AI

units.why: 'What you submit is your responsibility across these dimensions' makes the student answerable for all submitted content, so P29.
units.anchor: What you submit is your responsibility across these dimensions

units.why: 'AI can produce content that contains inaccurate information, offensive language/images, and biased or unethical representations' says output can be wrong or biased, so P31 informs (bias also appears, which P31 covers).
units.anchor: AI can produce content that contains inaccurate information, offensive language/images, and biased or unethical representations

units.why: 'Do not enter private, sensitive, or copyrighted data from others into AI tools without their consent' protects others' data, so P50 with must-not.
units.anchor: Do not enter private, sensitive, or copyrighted data from others into AI tools without their

units.why: 'Provide clear attribution of your sources' is a rule to attribute AI use, so P24 with must.
units.anchor: Provide clear attribution of your sources

units.why: 'Any assignments that utilize Generative AI without attribution ... can be seen as potential academic dishonesty' makes nondisclosure the violation, so P28 (P36 also fits but the key point is that missing attribution is what is penalized).
units.anchor: Any assignments that utilize Generative AI without attribution per the guidelines shared in this course

units.why: 'If AI usage is not permitted in your course, communicate your reasoning to your students' tells instructors to explain a ban, so P66.
units.anchor: communicate your reasoning to your students

units.why: Sample reason 'assignments in this course have been designed to ensure that you personally develop and demonstrate the knowledge and skills ... without the use of Generative AI' gives the skill-building rationale for a ban, so P41.
units.anchor: ensure that you personally develop and demonstrate the knowledge and skills associated with the learning

units.why: Sample reason 'its use is viewed as counter to the specific learning objectives of this course' justifies a ban by learning goals, so P41.
units.anchor: its use is viewed as counter to the specific learning objectives of this course

units.why: Sample reason 'Content in this course is private, sensitive, or copyrighted and should never be entered into a Generative AI tool' bans uploading course content, so P49.
units.anchor: should never be entered into a Generative AI tool

units.why: 'encourage students to speak with you directly to ensure their self-study does not interfere with graded or ungraded work' tells an instructor with a ban to invite students to discuss self-study use, so P10; here the instructor prompts the student.
units.anchor: encourage students to speak with you directly to ensure their self-study does not interfere
units.fit_note: Addressed to the instructor, who invites students to talk about self-study use, rather than to students who are unsure.

documents.title: AI Squared in Student Learning
tiers: Allowed for specific assignments, projects, or tasks
documents.summary: The School of Engineering's AI Squared page walks instructors through setting an AI policy: review learning goals, weigh detectors, redesign assignments and use sample statements. It offers four sample tiers and gives real course statements from engineering departments including COEN 11, COEN 346 and ELEN/COEN 21.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'a "one-size-fits-all" approach to syllabus statements is not suitable' and offers four scenario templates (prohibited, specific assignments, prior permission, attribution) plus course examples that differ from ban to encouragement, so the school sets no stance itself: delegates with tiers.

units.why: 'think about whether the use of generative AI tools in your course would support the learning goals' tells instructors to start from learning goals when deciding, so P04 with should.
units.anchor: think about whether the use of generative AI tools in your course would support the

units.why: 'It is important to examine the learning outcomes of your courses and adopt a suitable AI policy' advises each instructor to set a policy fitted to outcomes, so P04 with should.
units.anchor: It is important to examine the learning outcomes of your courses and adopt a suitable

units.why: 'there are none that are highly recommended in industry with a high accuracy rate' says detectors are unreliable, so P39 informs.
units.anchor: there are none that are highly recommended in industry with a high accuracy rate

units.why: 'to circumvent detection would be to replace variable names and values to less popular terms' shows code detectors are easy to evade, so P39 informs.
units.anchor: to circumvent detection would be to replace variable names and values to less popular terms

units.why: 'the issue will be trusting their result accuracy' while 'these tools can be used' states detectors may be used but are not trustworthy, so P39 informs.
units.anchor: the issue will be trusting their result accuracy

units.why: 'It might take using two or more tools in conjunction to further increase result accuracy' suggests using several detectors together to identify misuse, so P40 with may.
units.anchor: using two or more tools in conjunction to further increase result accuracy

units.why: Names GPTZero and Originality.ai as the detectors 'that have reputation for having the most accurate results', pointing instructors to specific tools, so P40 informs.
units.anchor: AI detectors that have reputation for having the most accurate results

units.why: 'Having students complete assignments and exams during class (in person)' is listed as a way to design assignments for the AI era, so P33 (more in-class unassisted assessment) with may.
units.anchor: Having students complete assignments and exams during class (in person).

units.why: 'Asking more nuanced questions that may be beyond the capabilities of the current AI tools' redesigns assignments around AI, so P35 with may.
units.anchor: Asking more nuanced questions that may be beyond the capabilities of the current AI tools.

units.why: 'Requiring students to show intermediate results of their assignments or projects before they submit' is a process-based redesign, so P35 with may.
units.anchor: Requiring students to show intermediate results of their assignments or projects before they submit their

units.why: 'Supplementing written assignments with additional oral presentations, flowcharts, concept maps, group work, case studies' adds formats where students show understanding; P34 covers oral and demo checks but this list also has non-oral formats.
units.anchor: Supplementing written assignments with additional oral presentations, flowcharts, concept maps, group work, case studies
units.fit_note: Includes non-oral formats (flowcharts, concept maps, group work, case studies) besides oral presentations.

units.why: 'You may not enter internal, sensitive or restricted data into any generative AI tool or service' bans entering protected data, so P50 with must-not.
units.anchor: You may not enter internal, sensitive or restricted data into any generative AI tool or

units.why: 'It is advisable for users to independently verify information obtained from generative AI' advises checking output, so P31 with should.
units.anchor: It is advisable for users to independently verify information obtained from generative AI

units.why: 'Generative AI may inadvertently mirror biases present in its training data' names bias as a risk, so P53 informs.
units.anchor: Generative AI may inadvertently mirror biases present in its training data

units.why: 'It is important to critically assess and place into context the responses generated by generative AI' asks users to evaluate output critically, so P31 with should.
units.anchor: critically assess and place into context the responses generated by generative AI

units.why: 'generative AI may produce or respond to content that is offensive, inappropriate, or breaches ethical standards' lists inappropriate content as a harm, so P53 informs.
units.anchor: generative AI may produce or respond to content that is offensive, inappropriate, or breaches ethical

units.why: 'a "one-size-fits-all" approach to syllabus statements is not suitable since each discipline and course has its own unique goals' leaves rules to each course, so P04 informs.
units.anchor: a "one-size-fits-all" approach to syllabus statements is not suitable

units.why: 'SCU's Academic Integrity policy underscores ... each instructor's responsibility to clearly communicate our own policies in the syllabus' requires syllabus communication, so P09 (stated as an existing policy requirement).
units.anchor: clearly communicate our own policies in the syllabus

units.why: 'be as specific as possible in addressing questions such as: Under what circumstances are generative AI tools allowed?' asks instructors to state when AI is allowed, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: be as specific as possible in addressing questions such as

units.why: 'What is the rationale or justification behind this policy?' is a question a syllabus should answer, so instructors explain their reasons: P66.
units.anchor: What is the rationale or justification behind this policy?
units.fit_note: Phrased as a question the syllabus statement should address.

units.why: 'What are the consequences for students violating the course policy?' asks syllabi to state consequences; P37 (state penalties in advance) is closest.
units.anchor: What are the consequences for students violating the course policy?
units.fit_note: Asks that consequences be stated; it names no actual penalty.

units.why: 'Where and how should students disclose their use of AI?' asks syllabi to specify disclosure, so P24 (disclosure) is nearest.
units.anchor: Where and how should students disclose their use of AI?
units.fit_note: A prompt for instructors to specify disclosure, not a disclosure requirement itself.

units.why: 'What are other forms of assistance and collaborative efforts acceptable? Identify the assignments for which such assistance is permitted' asks instructors to specify allowed help per assignment, so P04.
units.anchor: Identify the assignments for which such assistance is permitted.

units.why: 'Instructors may consider different possible scenarios below and adapt the sample statements' offers four templates (prohibited, specific assignments, prior permission, attribution), so P05 informs.
units.anchor: Instructors may consider different possible scenarios below and adapt the sample statements

units.why: Sample 'ChatGPT ... is not allowed in this class for any part of a graded assignment, including generation of ideas, writing of text, rewriting your own work, or generating computer code' is a total ban, so P01.
units.anchor: is not allowed in this class for any part of a graded assignment

units.why: Sample 'Doing so is considered a violation of SCU’s Academic Integrity and suspected use will be reported to the Office of Student Life' treats use as misconduct, so P36.
units.anchor: Doing so is considered a violation of SCU’s Academic Integrity

units.why: Sample 'you are permitted to utilize ChatGPT or similar AI generation tools, but only for designated assignments' allows AI per assignment, so P04.
units.anchor: you are permitted to utilize ChatGPT or similar AI generation tools, but only for designated
